milestones.title: Tenochtitlan founded on Lake Texcoco
milestones.detail: The Mexica settle an island in Lake Texcoco. The exact date is unclear; 13 March 1325 is the traditional date adopted for the city's 600th anniversary in 1925.

milestones.title: Great Temple rededicated in its final form
milestones.detail: The Templo Mayor, rebuilt six times since the founding, is dedicated in December 1487 and dominates the walled sacred precinct at the centre of the island city.

milestones.title: Cortés enters Tenochtitlan
milestones.detail: Hernán Cortés arrives on 8 November 1519 and meets Moctezuma II in a city of perhaps 200,000 people, among the largest in the world at the time.

milestones.title: Fall of Tenochtitlan
milestones.detail: After a siege the city surrenders on 13 August 1521. It is nearly destroyed, and the Spanish rebuild it on the same site as Mexico City.

milestones.title: Capital of the Viceroyalty of New Spain
milestones.detail: The Crown makes New Spain a viceroyalty and Mexico City its capital, with the viceroy's palace on the main square.

milestones.title: Work begins on the Metropolitan Cathedral
milestones.detail: Construction of the cathedral starts on the former Aztec sacred precinct; it is built in sections until 1813.

milestones.title: The great flood
milestones.detail: Rains inundate the capital in 1629 and flood waters stay for several years, prompting debate about moving the city and new drainage works (the Desagüe).
milestones.source: Hoberman, Louisa Schell (1974), 'Bureaucracy and Disaster: Mexico City and the Flood of 1629', Journal of Latin American Studies 6(2), via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Mexico_City

milestones.title: Revillagigedo census counts 112,926 residents
milestones.detail: The most detailed colonial census of the city, ordered by Viceroy Revillagigedo, records 112,926 inhabitants.
milestones.source: Valdés, Dennis N. (1978), The Decline of the Sociedad de Castas in Mexico City (PhD dissertation, University of Michigan), Table 2.1, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Mexico_City

milestones.title: Independence: the Trigarante Army enters
milestones.detail: The Army of the Three Guarantees enters Mexico City on 27 September 1821, ending Spanish rule; the city becomes the capital of independent Mexico.

milestones.title: Federal District created
milestones.detail: On 18 November 1824 the territory around the city is organised as the Federal District; the urban area then covers roughly today's Cuauhtémoc borough.

milestones.title: Occupied by the United States Army
milestones.detail: After the battles of Molino del Rey and Chapultepec (8-15 September 1847) the US Army under Winfield Scott takes the capital and occupies it for about a year.

milestones.title: Railway to Veracruz opens
milestones.detail: The Mexican Railway main line from Mexico City to the port of Veracruz is dedicated on 1 January 1873 by President Lerdo de Tejada.

milestones.title: Grand drainage canal inaugurated
milestones.detail: The Desagüe, draining the closed Valley of Mexico, is inaugurated in 1900 under Porfirio Díaz, reducing the flooding that had plagued the city since Aztec times.

milestones.title: The Ten Tragic Days
milestones.detail: A coup d'état against President Francisco I. Madero is fought out in the city between 9 and 22 February 1913, the one major episode of the Mexican Revolution inside the capital.

milestones.title: Summer Olympic Games
milestones.detail: Mexico City becomes the first Latin American city to host the Olympics, which bring large new sporting facilities.

milestones.title: Metro opens
milestones.detail: The first metro line opens on 4 September 1969 with 12.7 km of route and 16 stations.

milestones.title: Earthquake devastates the centre
milestones.detail: A magnitude 8.0 earthquake on 19 September 1985 causes serious damage across Greater Mexico City and kills at least 5,000 people.

milestones.title: Federal District renamed Ciudad de México
milestones.detail: On 29 January 2016 the Federal District officially becomes Ciudad de México (CDMX), with greater autonomy.

notes: Start date: 1325 is the traditional founding date of Tenochtitlan, fixed in 1925 for the 600th anniversary; the exact year is not securely documented, so it is marked estimated. Mexico City is the same continuously occupied site. Pre-conquest population is contested: published estimates for Tenochtitlan in 1519 run from 80,000 (Chandler 1987) through 100,000-200,000 (Berdan 1982) and 212,500 (Smith 2005, used here) to 200,000-400,000 (Denevan 1992); no count exists. No estimate is given for 1325-1518. The post-conquest collapse (about 30,000 in 1524) and the dip after the 1629 flood are Chandler's estimates. An alternative figure from Gibson (The Aztecs under Spanish Rule, 1964) is perhaps 22,000 indigenous inhabitants plus 150 Spanish households in 1525. Colonial figures for 1689 and 1753 are contemporary estimates; 1790, 1811 and 1813 are city censuses. Definitions change in 1895: figures from 1895 to 1940 are national census counts for the whole Federal District (entity), not the built-up city, so the step from 250,000 (1875, Chandler, city) to 476,413 (1895) is partly definitional; Chandler's city-only figures are 368,000 (1900), 600,000 (1914) and 772,000 (1925). The census table was read from Spanish Wikipedia, which cites INEGI; INEGI's own tables were not opened. Landmarks: skyscraper heights and years are from the CTBUH Skyscraper Center. Heights for the cathedral, Angel of Independence, Palacio de Bellas Artes, La Nacional and the new Basilica are taken from Wikipedia articles without a primary citation and are marked estimated. Left out for lack of a sourced height: National Palace, Chapultepec Castle, Estadio Azteca, Torre Lotería Nacional (El Moro; CTBUH and other sources disagree).
